This is the first lesson of Digital Logic, and almost everything later leans on it. Binary,
octal and hexadecimal (next lesson) are just bases 2, 8 and 16. Fractions and fixed point
(Lesson 3) extend place value to the right of the point. Signed numbers (Lesson 4) reuse the
same digits with one place given a negative weight. Later chapters read counter states, memory
addresses and IEEE-754 fields with exactly the tools built here.

The idea: a digit counts bundles

attrs.title: Digits count bundles, positions name the bundle size

c:
Think of a shop that only uses bundles of three: loose items, packets of 3, boxes of 3 packets
(9 items), crates of 3 boxes (27 items). To record 46 items you fill crates first: one crate
(27), then two boxes (18), no packets, and one loose item. The record reads

Each position holds the number of bundles of one size, and the sizes grow by the same factor
(here 3) as you move left. A position can never hold 3 or more, because three of anything
would be packed into one bundle of the next size. That one rule, "pack as soon as you reach
the base", is all of positional notation. Our everyday decimal is the same shop with bundles
of ten.

An odometer is the same shop in motion. Watch a counter whose wheels only know the digits 0, 1
and 2: when a wheel would reach 3 it rolls back to 0 and nudges its neighbour forward.
Notice what the counter shows after three counts:

three and nothing loose, which is three. That is why "10" means

in every base:
ten in decimal, two in binary, sixteen in hexadecimal.

more digits
Digits ten to thirty-five are written A to Z, so in hexadecimal A = 10, B = 11, …, F = 15.

in base 5. Only the place values change.

blocks.name: summary
blocks.title: Binary, octal and hex on one card

c:
Binary is the language of the hardware, but long strings of bits are hard for people to read.
Octal and hexadecimal fix that, and they fix it

: because 8 and 16 are powers of 2,
you convert by cutting the bit string into groups, with no division at all. In this lesson you
learn why grouping works, how to do it without the classic off-by-a-group slip, how to move
between octal, hex and base 4 through binary, how to read a "powers of 16" sum straight off as
hex, and how to add, subtract and multiply directly in base 8 or 16.

gave the general tools: expand to read, divide to write. They
work for every base, but for bases 2, 4, 8 and 16 they are the slow road. Everything in later
chapters is written in these bases: memory addresses and instruction fields in hex, Unix
permissions in octal, K-map cells and register contents in binary. The 2's-complement patterns
of Lesson 4 are also usually given in hex.

The idea: cutting a cake in halves

You may cut a cake only in half, then cut pieces in half again, and so on. You can serve exactly
a half, a quarter, three-eighths, five-sixteenths: any sum of these binary pieces. But you can
never serve

one fifth of the cake, however many times you cut: you can only get
closer and closer (a quarter is too much, three-sixteenths too little, …).
That is binary fractions in a nutshell. The pieces available are

, and a value is exactly representable only if it is a finite sum of them. A base-10
"cake" can be cut into tenths, so it serves one fifth (0.2) easily, but it cannot serve one
third. Which fractions come out exactly depends on the base.

steps.caption: 0.625 × 2 = 1.25. The integer part 1 is the next bit after the point; keep the fraction 0.25 for the next round.
0.25 × 2 = 0.5. The integer part 0 is the next bit after the point; keep the fraction 0.5 for the next round.
0.5 × 2 = 1. The integer part 1 is the next bit after the point; keep the fraction 0 for the next round. The fraction left is 0, so the expansion stops: 0.625 has a finite binary form.

fixed-point-ruler.title: Fixed point: the range–resolution trade-off
fixed-point-ruler.intro: A number line from 0 to 16 with sixteen tick marks, one for each 4-bit pattern. Each step moves the binary point one place left.

elements.text: 4 bits, point moved: range shrinks, steps get finer

steps.caption: With 0 fraction bits (4.0 format) the 16 patterns are the multiples of 1 from 0 to 15: resolution 1, largest value 15 = 2⁴ − 1.
With 1 fraction bit (3.1 format) the 16 patterns are the multiples of 0.5 from 0 to 7.5: resolution 0.5, largest value 7.5 = 2³ − 0.5.
With 2 fraction bits (2.2 format) the 16 patterns are the multiples of 0.25 from 0 to 3.75: resolution 0.25, largest value 3.75 = 2² − 0.25.
With 3 fraction bits (1.3 format) the 16 patterns are the multiples of 0.125 from 0 to 1.875: resolution 0.125, largest value 1.875 = 2¹ − 0.125.
The count of values never changes: n bits always give 2ⁿ = 16 patterns. Moving the point only trades range for resolution.

grouping-slider.intro: The seven bits 1011010. The red dot marks the radix point at the right end. Dashed cells on the left are padding zeros that will appear when a group runs short.

elements.text: Grouping the bits of (1011010)₂ from the right

steps.caption: Start at the radix point (here, just right of the last bit) and cut off three bits: 010. Three bits make one octal digit, and 010 is 2.
The next three bits to the left, 011, are the octal digit 3.
Only one bit, 1, is left. Pad it on the left with two zeros (that adds nothing to the value) to make 001 = 1.
Read the groups left to right: (1011010)₂ = (132)₈. Check: 64 + 24 + 2 = 90.
Now regroup in fours for hexadecimal, again starting at the point: 1010 is A.
The last three bits 101 need one padding zero: 0101 = 5. So (1011010)₂ = (5A)₁₆ = 5·16 + 10 = 90.

hex-nibble-table.title: The sixteen hex digits as 4-bit groups, with their count of 1s
hex-nibble-table.intro: Two tables. Left: hex digits 0 to 7, right: 8 to F. Each row gives the digit, its four bits, how many of those bits are 1, and its decimal value. For example 7 is 0111 with three 1s, and F is 1111 with four 1s.

horner-chain.title: Horner's chain: (257)₈ to decimal
horner-chain.intro: Start with a running total of 0. Each arrow will multiply the total by the base 8 and add one digit.

elements.text: Horner's chain for (257)₈: multiply by 8, add the next digit

steps.caption: Take the running total 0, multiply by 8 and add the next digit 2: 0 × 8 + 2 = 2.
Take the running total 2, multiply by 8 and add the next digit 5: 2 × 8 + 5 = 21.
Take the running total 21, multiply by 8 and add the next digit 7: 21 × 8 + 7 = 175.
Every digit has been used, so the last total is the value: (257)₈ = 175. The same total comes from 2·64 + 5·8 + 7, but without writing any powers.

octal-hex-bridge.title: The binary bridge from octal to hex
octal-hex-bridge.intro: The octal numeral 546, one box per digit. Binary and hex rows will appear under it.

elements.text: Octal → binary → hexadecimal, never through decimal

steps.caption: Write each octal digit as exactly three bits: 5 → 101, 4 → 100, 6 → 110. Each digit is replaced on its own; nothing carries between digits.
Now forget the old boundaries. Cut the bit string into fours, starting from the right end (the radix point).
The leftmost group has only one bit, so pad it with three zeros on the left: 0001.
Read each four-bit group as one hex digit: 0001 → 1, 0110 → 6, 0110 → 6.

odometer-rollover.title: An odometer that rolls over at 3
odometer-rollover.intro: Four counter wheels, all at 0. Under each wheel is the place value it stands for: 27, 9, 3 and 1.

elements.text: A base-3 counter (each wheel shows 0, 1 or 2)

steps.caption: One count: the right wheel moves from 0 to 1.
Two counts: the right wheel shows 2, the largest digit base 3 allows.
Three counts: the right wheel cannot show 3, so it rolls back to 0 and pushes the next wheel on by one. The display reads 10, which in base 3 means one three and no ones.
Jump ahead to 26 counts: every wheel shows its largest digit, 222. That is 2·9 + 2·3 + 2 = 26 = 3³ − 1.
One more count makes every wheel roll over in turn, and the carry ripples to a new wheel: 1000 in base 3 is 3³ = 27. In any base, 1 followed by k zeros is b to the power k.

place-value-strip.title: Place value: the same digits in base 3 and base 5
place-value-strip.intro: The digits 1 2 0 1 in four cells. Above each cell is its place value in base 3, a power of 3 that grows from right to left.

steps.caption: The first digit is 1 and sits in the 3³ = 27 place, so it adds 1 × 27 = 27. Running total: 27.
The second digit is 2 and sits in the 3² = 9 place, so it adds 2 × 9 = 18. Running total: 45.
The third digit is 0 and sits in the 3¹ = 3 place, so it adds 0 × 3 = 0. Running total: 45.
The fourth digit is 1 and sits in the 3⁰ = 1 place, so it adds 1 × 1 = 1. Running total: 46. So (1201)₃ = 46.
Now keep the same four digits but switch the base to 5. Only the place values change: 125, 25, 5 and 1.
Weighting each digit again: 125 + 50 + 0 + 1 = 176. Same digits, larger base, larger value: (1201)₅ = 176.

radix-solutions-grid.title: Counting radix solutions: every candidate pair, with the invalid ones explained
radix-solutions-grid.intro: Two tables of candidate pairs. A tick marks a pair that satisfies the equation and every digit limit. A cross names the rule the pair breaks: y = 1 is not a base, the digit 8 needs y ≥ 9, and the digit 4 needs x ≥ 5.

recurring-loop.title: Why 0.1 recurs in binary
recurring-loop.intro: The same doubling method as for 0.625, applied to 0.1. Watch the fraction that is kept after each row.

elements.text: 0.1 to binary never stops: the fraction comes back

steps.caption: The fraction left over is 0.2 again, the same as after the first row. From here the same four rows repeat for ever, so the bits 0011 repeat for ever.
So 0.1 = (0.0 0011 0011 0011 …)₂, a recurring binary fraction. Any finite number of bits only approximates it.

repeated-division-ladder.title: Repeated division: 2748 to hexadecimal
repeated-division-ladder.intro: We will divide by 16 again and again. Each remainder becomes one hex digit.

elements.text: Convert 2748 to base 16: divide by 16, keep the remainder

steps.caption: Divide 2748 by 16: quotient 171, remainder 12, which is written C in hex. This first remainder is the units digit.
Divide 171 by 16: quotient 10, remainder 11, which is written B in hex. Carry on with the quotient.
Divide 10 by 16: quotient 0, remainder 10, which is written A in hex. The quotient is now 0, so we stop.
The first remainder is the lowest digit and the last remainder is the leading digit, so read the column from the bottom up: A, B, C.
